title: Running an Import and Export Operation
grammar: Present simple vs present continuous in operations
objective: Coordinate a live import/export operation using intermediate business English.
grammarDetail: Present simple vs continuous. Use the simple for routines, the continuous for now. Example: We usually ship on Mondays. This week we are shipping on Wednesday because of the port strike.
grammarDeepDive: In operations, you constantly switch between describing what you always do and what is happening right now . The Present Simple covers routines, schedules and general facts: We ship forty containers a week. The warehouse closes at six. The Present Continuous covers actions in progress at the moment of speaking: We are dealing with a backlog this morning. James is leading the review right now.  The signal words help: always, usually, every Monday, normally point to the Simple; right now, this week, at the moment, today point to the Continuous. Both Eastwood ( Oxford Practice Grammar ) and Murphy ( English Grammar in Use ) emphasise that confusing the two tenses is one of the most common error

title: Choosing the Right Incoterms
objective: Select the right Incoterm for a given deal and justify it in English.
grammarDetail: Second conditional. Use if + past simple, would + verb for hypothetical situations. Example: If the shipment were lost, who would handle the claim? If we used DDP, we would carry all the risk.
grammarDeepDive: In trade, you constantly evaluate hypothetical scenarios: If we shipped FOB, who would handle the insurance? If the buyer chose DDP, would the seller bear all the risk? The Second Conditional is the grammar structure that powers these conversations. It uses if + past simple in the condition clause and would + base verb in the result clause. Eastwood ( Oxford Practice Grammar ) points out that the past tense in the 'if' clause does not refer to past time — it signals unreality or hypothesis. Murphy ( English Grammar in Use ) adds that 'were' can replace 'was' in formal contexts: If the shipment were lost, who would pay? title: Managing Global Supply Chains
objective: Discuss supply chain issues with suppliers and colleagues at an operational level.
grammarDetail: Linking words. Use because for reason, so for result, although for contrast. Example: The container is delayed because of port congestion, so we will re-route it, although it will cost a little more.
grammarDeepDive: Clear communication in supply chain management depends on showing the reason , the result , and the contrast between events. Three linking words do most of this work: because introduces the reason ( The shipment is delayed because of port congestion ), so introduces the result ( The port is congested, so we are re-routing ), and although introduces a contrast or surprise ( Although the delay looks bad, the customer is calm ). Eastwood ( Oxford Practice Grammar ) notes that these three connectors cover most of the logical linking a business professional needs at intermediate level. Murphy ( English Grammar in Use ) adds that although can appear at the start or in the middle of a sentence, but

title: Customs Clearance in Practice
grammar: Passive voice with modals — must be, can be
objective: Handle a customs clearance process and talk about it professionally.
grammarDetail: Passive with modals. Use must be / can be / will be + past participle . Example: The HS code must be checked twice. The shipment can be released once the correction is filed.
grammarDeepDive: Customs clearance is full of processes where the action matters more than the person doing it. That is why the passive voice with modals is so natural in this context: The HS code must be checked. The shipment can be released. The documents will be reviewed. The focus is on what happens to the shipment, not on who does it. Eastwood ( Oxford Practice Grammar ) explains that the structure is straightforward: modal + be + past participle . The modal carries the meaning — must for obligation, can for possibility, will for future certainty. title: Using Letters of Credit Effectively
objective: Use a letter of credit in practice and spot the most common errors.
grammarDetail: Relative clauses. Use which/that for things, whose for possession. Example: The LC, which the bank issued yesterday, has a clause whose dates are impossible.
grammarDeepDive: When you describe the terms of a letter of credit, you often need to add information about a specific document, clause, or person. Relative clauses let you do this in one smooth sentence instead of two choppy ones: The LC has a clause that cannot be met is clearer than The LC has a clause. The clause cannot be met.  Eastwood ( Oxford Practice Grammar ) distinguishes two types: defining clauses (with that ) identify which thing you mean — The documents that match the LC will be paid . Non-defining clauses (with which , set off by commas) add extra information — The LC, which was issued yesterday, has three errors. title: Bank Guarantees That Protect You
grammar: Modal verbs of obligation — must, have to, should
objective: Discuss and negotiate bank guarantees for real projects.
grammarDetail: Obligation modals.  Must and have to express strong obligation; should is advice. Example: The guarantee must cover the whole project. You should ask for 10% of the contract value, not 50%.
grammarDeepDive: In trade finance, precision matters — and so does the language you use to express rules, requirements and recommendations. Must expresses a strong internal obligation or a rule you believe in: The guarantee must cover the full project period.  Have to expresses an external requirement — something imposed by a contract, a regulation or a counterparty: We have to submit the bond before the tender deadline.  Should is softer — it gives advice or a recommendation: You should ask for 10%, not 50%.  In practice, must and have to are often interchangeable in business English, but there is a subtle difference. When a Czarnikow trader says 'We must hedge this exposure' , it sounds like a personal con

title: Documentary Collections in Practice
objective: Run a documentary collection and discuss it confidently.
grammarDetail: Used to vs be used to.  Used to + infinitive = past habit. Be used to + -ing = familiar with now. Example: We used to use only LCs. Now we are used to running collections as well.
grammarDeepDive: In trade finance, processes change over time — and we need language to talk about past habits and current familiarity. Used to + infinitive describes something that happened regularly in the past but no longer happens: We used to send all collections by post; now we use SWIFT. It only exists in the past tense. There is no present form of 'used to' in this sense.  Be used to + noun/-ing describes something you are accustomed to — familiar and comfortable with: Emily is used to handling documentary collections for French buyers. This form works in any tense: I am used to it , I was used to it , I will get used to it . Both Eastwood's Oxford Practice Grammar and Murphy's English Grammar in Use

title: Structuring Trade Credit
grammar: Linking words — however, therefore, in addition
objective: Design and explain trade credit terms for a real customer.
grammarDetail: Linking words. Use however for contrast, therefore for result, in addition for more. Example: The buyer has a strong record; however, the amount is large. Therefore, we will set a limit. In addition, we will add a 2% early payment discount.
grammarDeepDive: Clear business communication depends on showing how ideas connect. Three linking words are essential for trade finance professionals at Czarnikow: however (contrast), therefore (result/consequence), and in addition (adding information). These words signal to the listener or reader exactly how your next point relates to the previous one.  However introduces a contrast or an unexpected turn: The customer has a strong history; however, their market is volatile.  Therefore introduces a logical consequence: Exposure is rising; therefore, we must tighten the terms.  In addition adds a supporting point: We offer Net 30; in addition, we provide an early payment discount. Eastwood's Oxford Practice G

title: International Payments: Speed, Cost and Risk
objective: Choose the right international payment method for a given situation.
grammarDetail: Comparatives and superlatives.  faster, more reliable, the cheapest, the most transparent . Example: SWIFT is the most reliable but not the cheapest. The fintech rail is faster and more transparent.
grammarDeepDive: When choosing an international payment method, you constantly compare options. English has two systems for comparison. Short adjectives (one syllable, or two syllables ending in -y) add -er for comparatives and -est for superlatives: fast → faster → the fastest; cheap → cheaper → the cheapest . Long adjectives (two or more syllables) use more and the most : reliable → more reliable → the most reliable; transparent → more transparent → the most transparent . Three adjectives are irregular and must be memorised: good → better → the best; bad → worse → the worst; far → further → the furthest . title: FX Risk: Managing Currency Exposure
objective: Describe and manage currency exposure in a trade business.
grammarDetail: Present perfect continuous.  has/have been + -ing for actions starting in the past and still going. Example: We have been running on 5% margins all year. They have been watching the pound-dollar rate closely.
grammarDeepDive: In FX risk management, many actions are ongoing — they started in the past and are still happening now. The present perfect continuous (have/has been + verb-ing) is the perfect tense for this: We have been hedging our BRL exposure for six months. This tells us the hedging started six months ago and is still going on today. The structure is straightforward: subject + have/has + been + verb-ing . Use for to express duration ( for three months ) and since to express a starting point ( since January ). Eastwood's Oxford Practice Grammar and Murphy's English Grammar in Use both emphasise the contrast with the present perfect simple: I have hedged the exposure (completed action) vs I have been hed

title: Negotiating Payment Terms That Work
objective: Negotiate payment terms using trade-offs and real business English.
grammarDetail: First conditional. Use if + present, will + verb for realistic negotiation. Example: If you pay within 10 days, we will give you a 2% discount. If you need 120 days, we will need a higher price.
grammarDeepDive: The first conditional is the negotiator's best friend. It describes real, likely outcomes: if something happens, something else will happen . At Czarnikow, payment terms are negotiated daily, and the first conditional is the structure that makes trade-offs visible. Instead of demanding or refusing, you state the consequence: If you extend to 90 days, we will need a higher price . The other side can then decide. The structure is straightforward: if + present simple in the condition clause, will + base verb in the result clause. You can reverse the order: We will offer a discount if you pay within 10 days . title: Running Cross-Border Transactions
objective: Manage the operational side of cross-border deals end-to-end.
grammarDetail: Reported speech. Shift the tense back one step. Example: Sales said, 'The terms have changed.' → Sales said that the terms had changed.
grammarDeepDive: Reported speech is how we pass information from one team to another — and in cross-border operations, that happens dozens of times a day. When sales tells operations that the terms have changed , and operations tells finance the same thing, accuracy matters. In English, reported speech requires a tense shift : the verb moves one step back in time. 'The terms have changed' becomes 'Sales said that the terms had changed.'  The rules are consistent: present simple becomes past simple, present perfect becomes past perfect, 'will' becomes 'would', and 'can' becomes 'could'. title: Managing Risk in International Trade
objective: Describe and manage the main risks of international trade in practice.
grammarDetail: Passive voice.  is + past participle (present), was + past participle (past). Example: The shipment is insured. The risk was assessed last quarter.
grammarDeepDive: In risk management, the passive voice is the default register. Reports say 'The risk was assessed' , not 'Sophie assessed the risk' , because the focus is on the process, not the person. At Czarnikow, where risk registers, insurance certificates, and compliance reports are written every week, passive voice is not optional — it is expected. The structure is simple: subject + be + past participle . For present passive: is/are + past participle ( The shipment is insured ). For past passive: was/were + past participle ( The risk was assessed last quarter ). Eastwood ( Oxford Practice Grammar ) notes that the passive is especially common when the agent is obvious, unknown, or unimportant. Murphy

title: Due Diligence in Practice
objective: Run a basic due diligence process on a new partner.
grammarDetail: Reported questions. Use affirmative word order and shift the tense back. Example: "Does the company exist?" → She asked whether the company existed.
grammarDeepDive: Due diligence is built on questions: Does the company exist? Who owns it? Is anyone sanctioned? In English, when you report these questions to a colleague or in a compliance note, the structure changes. The word order becomes affirmative (no inversion), the tense shifts back, and you use whether or if for yes/no questions. Getting this right matters because compliance reports are legal documents — imprecise language is risky. For wh-questions, keep the question word but change the order: 'Who owns the company?' becomes 'She asked who owned the company.' For yes/no questions, add whether or if : 'Is the name on the watchlist?' becomes 'He asked whether the name was on the watchlist.' Eastwood

title: Navigating Sanctions Compliance
grammar: Third conditional — would have + past participle
objective: Apply sanctions compliance principles in real trade situations.
grammarDetail: Third conditional.  if + past perfect, would have + past participle for unreal past. Example: If we had screened again at payment time, we would have caught the change.
grammarDeepDive: The third conditional is the language of lessons learned. It describes unreal past situations — things that did not happen but could have, and what the result would have been. In sanctions compliance, this is critical: If we had screened again at payment time, we would have caught the change. The sentence analyses a failure and shows what should have been done differently. The structure is: if + past perfect (had + past participle), would have + past participle . Both clauses look into the past at something that did not happen. Eastwood ( Oxford Practice Grammar ) calls this the 'impossible past conditional' because the condition can no longer be fulfilled. Murphy ( English Grammar in Use )

title: Negotiating International Contracts
objective: Negotiate and draft key clauses of a trade contract.
grammarDetail: Defining vs non-defining relative clauses. Defining clauses have no commas and are essential. Non-defining have commas and add extra info. Example: The clause that defines force majeure is essential. The contract, which runs to 40 pages, will be reviewed next week.
grammarDeepDive: In English, relative clauses give extra information about a noun. The critical distinction — especially in legal and business English — is between defining (restrictive) and non-defining (non-restrictive) clauses. A defining clause tells you which one: The clause that covers force majeure is on page 12. Remove it and you lose the meaning. A non-defining clause adds extra information that is useful but not essential: The contract , which runs to 40 pages, was signed in March. Remove it and the sentence still makes sense. The punctuation rule is simple but powerful: no commas for defining clauses, commas for non-defining clauses. In contracts, this distinction can change legal meaning. Both Ox

title: Managing Working Capital in Trade
objective: Manage working capital in a live trade operation.
grammarDetail: Quantifiers.  Much/little for uncountable; many/few for countable. Example: We have many overdue invoices but little cash in the account. There are a few quick wins.
grammarDeepDive: Quantifiers tell us how much or how many of something we have. In business English — especially in finance — choosing the right quantifier is essential for accuracy. The rule is straightforward: much and little go with uncountable nouns (cash, inventory, time, capital), while many and few go with countable nouns (invoices, customers, days, suppliers). There is a subtle but important difference between few and a few . Few means 'almost none' and is negative: Few customers paid on time (a problem). A few means 'some' and is positive: A few customers paid early (a good sign). The same logic applies to little vs a little . Both Eastwood ( Oxford Practice Grammar , Unit 72) and Murphy ( English G

title: Cash Flow in Cross-Border Business
grammar: Future forms — will, going to, present continuous
objective: Forecast and manage cross-border cash flow.
grammarDetail: Future forms.  Will for decisions now, going to for plans, present continuous for arranged events. Example: We will cover the shortfall. We are going to delay a payment. The bank is transferring funds on Monday.
grammarDeepDive: English has three main ways to talk about the future, and each carries a different meaning. Will is for spontaneous decisions ( I'll call the bank now ), promises ( We will cover the shortfall ), and predictions based on opinion ( I think they will pay late ). Going to is for plans already decided ( We are going to delay the payment ) and predictions based on evidence ( Look at these numbers — we are going to need a buffer ). Present continuous is for fixed arrangements with a specific time and place ( The bank is transferring the funds on Monday ). In cash flow forecasting, precision matters. title: Financing Trade in Emerging Markets
grammar: Expressing opinion — I'd argue, I'd say, in my view
objective: Discuss how to finance trade in emerging markets.
grammarDetail: Expressing opinion politely. Start with I'd argue, I'd say, in my view to soften strong views. Example: I'd argue that local relationships matter more than product choice.
grammarDeepDive: In international business, how you say something matters as much as what you say. Blunt opinions — This is wrong , You should do it differently — can damage relationships, especially across cultures. English offers elegant softeners that let you state a strong opinion without sounding aggressive: I'd argue (strong but diplomatic), I'd say (conversational and mild), and in my view (formal and personal).  I'd argue uses the conditional ('I would argue') to signal that you are presenting an opinion, not a fact. It is the strongest of the three and works well when you want to challenge a prevailing view: I'd argue that relationships matter more than products.  I'd say is softer and more tentativ

title: Negotiating Across Borders
grammar: Hedging language — seem to, appear to, it might be
objective: Negotiate professionally across cultures and time zones.
grammarDetail: Hedging. Use seem to, appear to, it might be, it could be to avoid sounding final. Example: That seems to be their preference. It might be wise to ask again next week.
grammarDeepDive: Hedging is the art of saying something without saying it outright. In cross-cultural negotiation, it is essential. Seem to describes an impression: They seem to prefer a later delivery date.  Appear to is more formal and cautious: The buyer appears to be consulting their head office.  It might be introduces a possibility: It might be wise to wait before making a counter-offer.  Why hedge? Because in international business, stating things as facts when they are really impressions can cause offence or lock you into a position.
